title: Oncall cheatsheet: GPU replacement, cordon/drain and capacity add (draft)
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a compact, on-call friendly draft covering common infra failure workflows we hit most: replacing a failing GPU, cordon/drain node for maintenance, cluster recovery after partial outage, and quick capacity add (scale-out). Intended for SREs on rotation and platform engineers who need a fast checklist during incidents.

Status: draft — rough notes, TODOs inline. Use judgement; if unsure, escalate to on-call lead.

Quick triage (first 5 minutes)
- Channel: jump to incident Slack channel (prefilled from pager) and post short status.
- Observe: look at Console -> Cluster health, telemetry (node-exporter, GPU metrics), and recent autoscaler events.
- Severity decision: is user-facing latency/failed requests > threshold? If yes: P1.
- Snapshot: capture current kubectl get nodes -o wide, describe failing pods, and top pods by restarts. Paste into the channel.

Common sources of failures seen recently:
- Faulty GPU hardware causing machine to crash or be OOMed by the kernel (dmesg shows GPU fault).
- Driver/kernel mismatches after node kubelet upgrade.
- Burst traffic causing autoscaler to fail to provision due to quota/hard limits.
- Pod eviction deadlocks when KV cache is large (seen on long context jobs).

GPU replacement (field/remote) — high-level
1) Confirm hardware problem: check node logs: sudo dmesg | grep -i nvidia or check /var/log/syslog. Look for GPU ECC errors, driver crash reports.
2) If node still responding but GPU misbehaves, cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node>.
3) Drain safely: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m. Monitor evictions; if pods stuck in terminating > 5m, check finalizers.
4) If pods are stateful (model-serving state): follow stateful eviction playbook (note: patch config to route traffic to fallback model instance first).
5) If hardware needs replacement onsite: tag ticket for facilities with serial #, include exact node name and GPU model. If remote (colocation/cloud), open vendor ticket and request emergency RMA.
6) After physical swap, verify BIOS/driver: nvidia-smi shows expected devices; run a small perf test (curl internal perf endpoint) before uncordoning.
7) kubectl uncordon <node> and watch Pod startup (kubectl get pods -o wide).

Node cordon + drain checklist (quick)
- Pre-check: check scheduling pressure, cluster capacity (kubectl top nodes).
- Run: kubectl cordon <node> (add note to channel why).
- Drain with timeouts and watch critical pods: kubectl drain <node> --force? Avoid --force unless broken.
- If eviction stalls: check podDisruptionBudget (PDB), reduce PDB temporarily if safe (requires app owner approval).
- For DaemonSets: ensure pods re-created elsewhere or rely on daemonset affinity.
- Post-drain: perform maintenance (driver update, kernel rollback, hardware swap).
- Bring back: validate system metrics for 5–10m then kubectl uncordon.

Cluster recovery (partial outage)
- If multiple nodes fail or autoscaler stuck: check control plane health first (api-server, kube-controller-manager in Console).
- Check cloud provider quotas (GPUs, IPs): gcloud compute quotas or cloud provider console. Common root cause for failed scale-ups.
- If control plane healthy but pods pending: describe a pending pod to see nodeSelector/taints/insufficient resources.
- If autoscaler misconfigured: inspect cluster-autoscaler logs (kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler). If autoscaler scaled down too aggressively we roll back scale-down recommendation.
- To temporarily recover: manual node add (create nodepool / provision VMs with required labels). Use infra repo scripts: ./infra/tools/provision-nodepool.sh --type=gpu --count=3 --region=us-west1. (PR required for persistent changes).

Quick capacity add (emergency scale out)
- Validate quota first. If quota exhausted, contact cloud quotas team with the incident number.
- If quotas available: provision a small nodepool (1–3 nodes) with same labels: cloud cli + infra helper script above.
- Once nodes appear, untaint if necessary and allow pods to schedule.
- Watch autoscaler: it should stabilize and then we can scale down later.
- Post-incident: create a capacity plan ticket for next-day review.

Troubleshooting commands (cheat list)
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe node <node>
- kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep Pending
- kubectl logs -n <ns> <pod> -c <container>
- kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler
- nvidia-smi -q
- dmesg | grep -i nvidia
- gcloud compute instances describe <instance>

Observed failure modes and quick mitigations (notes from recent incidents)
- GPU memory ECC errors: immediate cordon, create RMA. Keep a warm spare pool for high-throughput clusters.
- Kubelet OOM/kube-proxy crash loops: roll back recent kubelet flags; if rollback not possible, drain and reprovision.
- Autoscaler hung: manual nodepool create and then investigate logs; often due to taints/labels mismatch on instance template.

Escalation matrix
- If hardware RMA needed: Facilities lead (Ava Martinez) and procurement.
- If cloud quota/limit: Infra platform owner (Ravi Patel) and cloud vendor support.
- If service-impacting and >30m unresolved: page SRE lead and Product on-call.

Post-incident review template (to fill quickly in channel after stabilization)
- Timeline: short bullet timeline (pager -> triage -> mitigation -> recovery).
- Root cause hypothesis (one or two sentences).
- Actions taken (what worked, what didn't).
- Customer impact (services affected, duration).
- Follow-ups / owners (e.g., replace node pool with new image: owner: infra-team).
- Known unknowns (next experiments needed).

Retrospective notes (examples from past incidents)
- We underestimated the time to provision GPUs in us-west because quota was near limit; add daily quota alert.
- Drains blocked by PDBs on critical workloads — need an agreed emergency PDB override process.
- On-call script: add an automated checklist that runs diagnostics and posts a gist to the channel (PR: #987).

Safety and do-not-do list
- DO NOT use kubectl drain --force unless you understand the implications (data loss for local storage).
- DO NOT bump driver versions mid-incident without testing on a canary node.
- DO escalate early if replacement timeline > 2 hours.

Open TODOs (draft action items)
- [ ] Add sampled diagnostics script to infra/tools and wire to Pager -> incident channel. (owner: Jordan Kim)
- [ ] Create playbook snippet for stateful model-serving eviction (owner: Sophie Nguyen)
- [ ] Add daily GPU quota telemetry and Slack alert (owner: Ravi Patel)

Appendix: useful links and snippets
- Infra repo PR for automated provisioner: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/987
- Recent incident review: confluence:incidents/2026-01-gpu-failure (draft)
- Slack archive channel: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C02SREONCALL

Notes to self: keep this as A4-friendly one-pager for phones. We should split the stateful eviction guidance into its own file and link here.
